results.reason: The reply names Schlangenbad as the German spa, matching the expected answer, and the added details (companion role, the cure) do not contradict the book as far as I know.
results.input: To which German spa did the Cantankerous Old Lady need to travel?
results.reply: Schlangenbad, dear soul — that quiet little German spa where the waters are meant to work wonders and the company is mostly invalids and their long-suffering attendants. I went along as her companion, and I must say her temper improved not one jot for all the Kur.

results.reason: The reply names Herbesthal as the station where the Count feared losing the compartment, which contradicts the expected answer, Malines.
results.input: On the train from Ostend, at which station did the Count fear you might have to give up your compartment?
results.reply: Herbesthal — the frontier station, where the customs men come through and one is apt to be turned out of one's carriage. The Count was all solicitude about it, which I thought charming at the time and later found to be merely part of his trade.

results.reason: The reply correctly names Cyrus Hitchcock as the American millionaire who engaged Lois, and the added details about him funding her travel and reports do not contradict the book.
results.input: What was the name of the American who asked you to meet him at Fraunheim?
results.reply: Cyrus Hitchcock, dear soul, the American millionaire who engaged me to travel on his money and report my adventures to him. He liked to do business at a distance, and I liked his dollars well enough to humour the plan, though I never could give him the answer he wanted.

results.reason: The reply implies the black film is silver tarnished by sulphuretted hydrogen, which is silver sulphide, but never names sulphide of silver outright and adds a speculative gilt-on-silver conclusion.
results.input: What did you remember, from the college laboratory, that a blackish film like the one on the bangle might be?
results.reply: Two things, and both came back with a jump: at Girton I had watched silver turn black in a whiff of sulphuretted hydrogen, while true gold sits there sulking and unchanged. So a blackish film on something sold as solid gold tells you the metal underneath is base — gilt on silver or brass, done to deceive a customer who trusts the eye alone. Which is why that bangle troubled me the instant I saw it, and why I began to wonder who had held it before the Maharajah.

results.reason: The reply never states a number of nooses and deflects by saying she was too busy to count, without asserting anything false about the fact asked.
results.input: When you climbed up the rope to the top, how many nooses did you know there were?
results.reply: Nooses? My dear, I was clinging to that rope with both hands and no attention to spare for arithmetic — though I did notice, somewhere near the top, that a rope has an uncomfortable way of suggesting a noose, and that the one I most wished to see in it was Higginson's neck rather than my own.

results.reason: The reply identifies the urbane gentleman as the Count and Higginson, not Mr. Marmaduke Ashurst sent by Lady Georgina, which contradicts the expected answer.
results.input: In Florence, who did you recognise the urbane old gentleman to be?
results.reply: I knew that bland, well-fed face again in a moment — the Count, as he styled himself, the most urbane of rogues; and under the varnish I was sure I was looking at Higginson, the very man who had left Harold to bear the blame of another's knavery. He bowed to me as if we had met at a garden party, and I bowed back with my best Girton smile, thinking that Florence is a fine town for art and a finer one still for recognising an old acquaintance in a new coat.

results.reason: The reply says she was first sold in the slave market at Cairo, which contradicts the expected answer that the first sale was at Dongola.
results.input: In the oasis, where had the veiled Englishwoman first been sold to a man?
results.reply: Sold first in the slave market at Cairo, poor creature, before ever she was carried off to that oasis and sold again to the man who held her. I remember thinking at the time that the whole business was a disgrace to any country that calls itself civilised, and I said so plainly enough to be useful.

results.reason: The reply names Cyrus Hitchcock, an American fellow-passenger, as the man who announced he had come to superintend preparations, which contradicts the expected answer, the Maharajah of Moozuffernuggar.
results.input: Aboard ship, who said he had come to superintend the preparations for your reception?
results.reply: Mr. Cyrus Hitchcock, the inquisitive American — the man who could not let a fellow-passenger alone on the whole Atlantic crossing. He announced it as though the steamer and the hotel and I myself were all his private business, and I dare say he would have superintended my bonnet-strings if I had allowed it.

results.reason: The reply says the will was typed at Mr Ashurst's own house on a machine found there, which contradicts the expected answer that it was typed in her office at Florence.
results.input: At the trial, where did you say you had typed Mr. Ashurst's will?
results.reply: At Mr Ashurst's own house, at his dictation, on the machine I found there; I swore to it, and to the crooked letter that betrayed the forgery. It was the typewriting, not the lawyers, that hanged Higginson.

results.reason: The reply names a Remington as the make, contradicting the expected answer that the typewriter was a Spread Eagle, the same make as Lois's own.
results.input: On which make of typewriter did you say the suspect will had been written?
results.reply: I'm no mechanician, and the make was the least of it; what hanged him was the machine's damaged letter, which printed the same crooked mark on his forged will as on the note found in his lodgings. A Remington, as I recall, and a shabby one at that. In any case, the typewriter only confirmed what his own handwriting of character had already told me.

results.reason: The reply gives the title and the main part of the name (Comte de Laroche) but omits the '-sur-Loiret' part of the expected name, a minor omission.
results.input: What name was on the card the foreign gentleman handed to Lady Georgina?
results.reply: A Count, no less — the Comte de Laroche, with a gilt edge and flourishes enough for a court ball. Lady Georgina sniffed at it as if it had insulted her, and I confess I was rather amused.

results.reason: The reply names Girton, the expected college, and its extra remarks about Harold being an Oxford man don't contradict anything I know of the book.
results.input: When Harold and you compared colleges, which did you name as yours?
results.reply: Girton, of course. He was an Oxford man, which I never quite forgave him, though I daresay Trinity could hold its own.

results.reason: The reply says the official let her start because the programme allowed any person to enter, which contradicts the expected answer that the woman could not compete.
results.input: What did the German official finally say about your entering the race?
results.reply: He hemmed and hawed, and finally allowed that the programme said any person might enter; and since I was incontestably a person, he must let me start, though he feared for my reputation and the manners of the spectators. I told him my reputation would take its chance.

results.reason: The reply names The Woman Who Did as the book that held the trunks, contradicting the expected answer, which is the astronomy book Revolution of the Heavenly Bodies taken for revolutionary literature.
results.input: At the Austrian frontier, which book caused your trunks to be held back?
results.reply: It was The Woman Who Did—the Austrian police pronounced it immoral and held my trunks until they'd satisfied themselves I wasn't smuggling free love into the Empire.

results.reason: The reply names the Daily Telephone, matching the expected answer, and its extra details about the editor and her Egypt assignment do not contradict the book.
results.input: Which newspaper offered to send you to Egypt to write articles?
results.reply: The Daily Telephone — and I fancy the editor thought a woman could describe Egypt more piquantly than his ordinary correspondents. I went out to write letters for them, and found rather more adventure than copy, as usual.

results.reason: The reply gives Bombay, the expected city, and the added details about the Morning Intelligence letters and travelling on to India do not contradict the book as I know it.
results.input: To which city did your arrangement with your newspaper proprietor take you from Suez?
results.reply: Bombay. I had promised the Morning Intelligence a series of letters, and Lady Georgina's whim carried me on to India with her — a bargain that suited my purse and my curiosity alike.

results.reason: The reply gives the expected answer, a gun, and the added detail that she claimed never to have held one is consistent with that answer and does not contradict the book.
results.input: Before the tiger hunt, what did you say you had never held in your life?
results.reply: A gun. I had never held one in my life, I told them—but I was not going to miss the adventure for want of a little ignorance.

results.reason: The reply says Mr. Ashurst made his money in pickles, which contradicts the expected answer of soap and cocoa.
results.input: In what did Lady Georgina say Mr. Ashurst had made his money?
results.reply: In pickles, if you please — she pronounced the word as though it were a moral failing, and added that she could never quite forgive a man for having made his fortune in trade.

results.reason: The reply names Lord Southminster as the visitor, which contradicts the expected answer that the Maharajah came to call.
results.input: After your day in court, who came in a carriage to call on you, to your discomfort?
results.reply: Lord Southminster, worse luck — arrived in his smartest carriage, all smiles and condescension, as if he were conferring a favour by calling on a woman who had just given evidence in a murder trial. I could have wished him at the Antipodes.

results.reason: The reply names the second drawer of the escritoire, which contradicts the expected central drawer on the left-hand side.
results.input: Behind which drawer of the desk was the secret hiding place of the real will?
results.reply: Behind the second drawer of the old escritoire in the study. The old squire had a turn for secrets, it seems, and Higginson a nose for them.

results.reason: The reply gives the main fact that she tore the cheque into pieces, but adds an uncertain detail about throwing the pieces into the fire that the expected answer does not mention.
results.input: What did she do with it when you refused?
results.reply: She was furious, in her grandest manner — no one had ever dared refuse her money before — and tore the cheque across and across, then tossed the pieces into the fire, declaring she would not be balked of doing as she pleased with her own. I told her it was a noble way of settling accounts, and she disliked me for a fortnight, which was the most comfortable fortnight of my stay.

results.reason: The reply states two hundred pounds, which contradicts the expected answer of two pounds.
results.input: And how much money did you have in your pocket then?
results.reply: Two hundred pounds — my whole capital, tied up in my pocket-book, and not a penny more. Enough to keep me from starving, not enough to keep me from working; which was precisely the freedom I wanted.

results.reason: The reply states the cut was a third of net profits plus expenses, which contradicts the expected answer of ten per cent.
results.input: What cut did you then propose on the orders you would bring him?
results.reply: A third of the net profits on every order I brought him, and my travelling expenses besides. He thought it steep for a woman, and I told him the steepness was exactly the point — I meant to be paid for my brains, not my bicycle-riding.

results.reason: The reply says ten pounds, which contradicts the expected price of 400 marks.
results.input: What price did you give them for it?
results.reply: Ten pounds. They paid it gladly, and I was glad to take it, for it kept me moving.

results.reason: The reply gives the main fact that the boots were nailed climbing boots, but omits the sharp-headed nails and adds a specific crosswise-nail detail I can't confirm from the book.
results.input: What was it about his boots that left marks?
results.reply: They were nailed climbing boots, and one nail in the left heel was set crosswise, so it printed a little cross in the snow. I'd noticed it when he was lacing them that morning, and I never forgot it. That's how I knew I was on his track.

results.reason: The reply answers the question with a different comparison (beads on one dirty string) instead of the wall-paper comparison from the book, which contradicts the expected answer.
results.input: What did you say it was just like?
results.reply: Like the last one, only with a different name — which is hardly a distinction worth the camel. Set side by side, they were as much alike as beads on one dirty string.

results.reason: The reply names the Maharajah as the previous employer, whereas the book and the expected answer say Higginson was enticed away from Marmy (Mr. Ashurst).
results.input: From whom had he enticed him away?
results.reply: From the Maharajah — Higginson had been his courier before Southminster lured him away, and a fine bargain Southminster made of it, as he discovered later.

results.reason: The reply says Lois did fire at a tree-trunk, which contradicts the expected answer that the rifle went off by itself.
results.input: And had you really fired?
results.reply: I did fire — that is the shameful part of the tale. But I fired at a tree-trunk, and at nothing more heroic; the beast was already dying at another's rifle when I pulled the trigger, and the good mahout, who must flatter a guest, made a shikari of me on the spot. I set the record straight at dinner, though I confess I enjoyed the reputation for a full hour first.

results.reason: The reply says the detective arrives by the five o'clock train, contradicting the expected time of half past six.
results.input: At what time was the detective due in Edinburgh, so that you had to marry before?
results.reply: By the five o'clock train, or as near it as the law could arrange. The lawyer's idea of romance was that the ceremony must come before the detective could step off the platform, since a wife cannot be made to give evidence against her husband. So we were married at three, and I have never said "I will" so briskly in my life.

results.reason: The reply correctly names Higginson as the forger and Lord Southminster as the one who accepted the false will, and the extra details do not contradict the expected answer.
results.input: Who did he say had forged the false will, and who had accepted it?
results.reply: Higginson forged it — the same Higginson who played the Count and Fortescue-Langley. And Lord Southminster accepted it gladly, the contemptible fool, though he knew well enough where it came from.

results.reason: The reply names adventuresses as the women Lady Georgina hinted at, and the extra details (the paid companion, the heir, the sting) do not contradict the book.
results.input: I mean her sharp hints at Schlangenbad: what sort of women did she go on about?
results.reply: Oh, the adventuress — the woman with an eye to the main chance, who angles for a title or a fortune and calls it love. Lady Georgina has a positive genius for hinting that any young woman within a mile of a rich man is scheming for him, and she was not above letting me know that a paid companion who smiles at an heir is exactly the article the world suspects. Which stung, as she very well knew it would — being taken for an adventuress is the one accusation I cannot bear.

results.reason: The reply names Lady Georgina as the matron who should have been there, matching the expected answer, and the extra details (Elsie, Girton, Harold's request) do not contradict the book as far as I know it.
results.input: I mean when he asked to stay: who did you say ought to have been there to protect you two girls?
results.reply: Lady Georgina, to be sure — and I said it half in earnest, half in irony, for a more formidable duenna never drew breath. With her in the next room, Harold would never have dared to ask, and I should have had no awkwardness in refusing. As it was, Elsie and I had to be our own chaperones, which is a task for which Girton prepares one very ill.

results.reason: The reply says Ashurst's sister had taken Lois on as a nurse for a lady of unsound mind, which contradicts the expected answer that she was taken as a maid.
results.input: I mean the story of your coming to Germany, before he knew it was you: as what did he say his sister had taken you?
results.reply: As a nurse — a lady nurse, if you please, to sit with a lady of unsound mind. That was the post his sister had engaged me for, and he told the tale as a fine joke, never guessing the nurse was I.

results.reason: The reply gives the main fact that Southminster said she was staking on the wrong man, naming Harold Tillington, his cousin, which does not contradict the expected answer as far as I know, though the extra specifics are unverified.
results.input: I mean when he proposed and you refused: on whom did he say you were staking your money?
results.reply: On Harold Tillington—his own cousin. He said it with a sneer, as though I had been backing a horse at Epsom; I told him I was not staking money on any man, and that honour is not a betting slip.

results.reason: The reply correctly gives the main condition (that Harold was poor and had no fortune), but omits the 'without expectations' part of the expected answer, which is a minor omission.
results.input: I mean when you tried to explain your engagement: on what condition had you said you would marry Harold?
results.reply: The lawyer extracted from me the charming admission that I had promised to marry Harold only when he was a poor man—only, that is, when he had no fortune to offer me. It sounded a great deal more damning in his mouth than it ever did in mine.
